segments.text: Usage: `rx.sh NAME BINARY SHA256`, with a spec file as input. Each line of the spec file is `tag|arguments of the binary` and gives one process. `Marker file` in the comment is the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` (line 5). `CPUs 0-119 only` is set in line 17.
segments.heading: Header comment: usage

segments.text: `set -u`: the script stops when it uses a variable that was never set. The script does not use `set -e`. So a failed command does not stop it.

`M`: the path of the marker file. Then the three arguments:
- `name`: a part of the name of the result folder
- `BW`: the path of the binary to run
- `sha`: the sha256 that the binary must have

Marker check 1 of 3.
- Test: does the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` exist.
- On failure (the file exists): the script prints `RUNNING file present: stop` and ends with exit status 3. It has written no file at this point.
- Purpose: the script does not say who creates the file or what the file stands for.
segments.heading: Checks before the first process

segments.text:
Checksum check of the binary.
- Test: `sha256sum -c -` reads one line `checksum  path` from `echo`, computes the sha256 of the binary and compares it with the third argument. Its report goes to `/dev/null`, which discards it.
- On failure (the content differs, or the file cannot be read): the script prints `sha mismatch` and ends with exit status 2.
- Purpose: the script gives none. The caller chooses the expected value.

Result folder: `~/cache-perf/results/w120-<name>-<UTC time>`, for example `w120-T72L1-20261117T221329Z` [Ref1]. `mkdir -p` creates it. The time in the name is read here, before the wait of lines 14 and 15. So it is at least 5 s before the start of the first process.

Writes the file `env.txt` once, before any process. It holds, in this order:
- the UTC date and time (`date -u`)
- the release of the running Linux kernel (`uname -r`)
- the content of `/proc/loadavg`
- the logged-in users, one line each (`who`). It prints nothing when nobody is logged in.
- a header line and the 5 processes with the highest %CPU (`ps` sorted by `pcpu`, then `head -6`)
- the word `binary`, the path of the binary and the expected sha256

Reads the input (the spec file) line by line.
- `IFS='|'` splits each line at the first `|`. The text before it goes to `tag`. The rest of the line goes to `args`.
- `-r` keeps each backslash as it is.
- Line 12 skips a line with an empty tag, for example an empty line.
- Each of the three spec files of the rerun holds one line. So each call of rx.sh starts one process [Ref2].
segments.heading: Loop: one process per spec line

segments.text: Marker check 2 of 3, before each process. When the marker file exists, the script prints `marker: stop` and ends with exit status 3.

Wait for at most 2 runnable tasks, with at most 40 tries.
- Test: `cut -d' ' -f4 /proc/loadavg` takes the fourth field, for example `1/1019`. `cut -d/ -f1` keeps the number before the slash. This is the number of tasks that are runnable now [Ref5].
- When the number is 2 or less, the loop ends immediately.
- If not, the script sleeps 1 s and tests again.
- On failure (still above 2 after 40 tries, about 40 s): the loop ends too. The script goes on and starts the process. It prints no message.
- Purpose: the script does not say why the limit is 2.
A fixed pause of 5 s after the wait.

Appends one `launch` line to `launches.txt`: the tag, the UTC time (hours:minutes:seconds), the content of `/proc/loadavg`, the number of logins, and the arguments. This is the last reading of the machine state before the process starts.

Starts the binary in the background (`&`). The script goes on immediately.
- CPU list: `taskset -c 0-119` allows the new process to run on the CPUs 0 to 119 only. Then `taskset` replaces itself with the binary in the same process. So the process id of line 18 is the process id of the binary.
- Arguments: `$args` has no quotes. So the shell splits it at the spaces, and each word becomes one argument of the binary.
- Output: the standard output of the binary goes to `<tag>.csv` in the result folder. `>` creates the file, or empties it when it exists. Error messages are appended to `stderr.txt` (`2>>`).
- Input: `/dev/null`, an empty input. So the binary cannot read the rest of the spec file, which is the input of the loop.
- rx.sh pins no thread. bwx12 pins each thread to one CPU of its `--cpus` argument [Ref3].
segments.heading: Start of the binary and wait for its end

segments.text:
Waits for the process and watches the marker file.
- `pid=$!` keeps the process id of the started process.
- `kill -0 $pid` sends no signal. It only tests whether the process still exists. The loop runs as long as it exists.
- Marker check 3 of 3, once per second: when the marker file exists, `kill $pid` sends the termination signal to the process. The script prints `marker: killed` and ends with exit status 3. It writes no `rc` line then.
- If the marker file does not exist, `sleep 1` waits 1 s.
- So rx.sh sees the end of the binary up to about 1 s late. This loop runs in the shell of rx.sh while the binary measures.

`wait $pid` returns the exit status of the binary. The script appends the line `rc <exit status> <tag> utc <time>` to `launches.txt`. It does not test the status, and it goes on with the next spec line. The time in this line can be about 1 s later than the real end of the process (the poll of line 19).

Prints a short summary to the standard output:
- `done` and the path of the result folder
- the number of non-empty lines of `launches.txt` (2 per finished process: one `launch` line and one `rc` line)
- every `rc` line whose status is not 0
- the size of `stderr.txt` in bytes
- the first 600 bytes of `stderr.txt`
- The exit status of rx.sh is the status of the last command, `head`. It does not depend on the exit status of the binary.
segments.heading: Summary and exit status
